answer:
What I ran: a line of 6 spins with H = ZZ on each neighbor pair plus X on each spin (J = 1, h = 1), all starting pointed up. I built 6 circuits for times 0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0. Each one steps the spins forward in small slices of 0.1 time units (a Trotter approximation). I sent all 6 circuits as one job (ID 01a16041-018c-730f-b5e1-dc7bbee9e916) to garnet:mock with 1000 shots each. The job cost no credits.

What a perfect quantum computer shows: the average magnetization starts at 1.00 and falls as the X term tips the spins and the ZZ term spreads that tipping along the line. Exact values are 1.00 at t=0, 0.74 at 0.4, 0.34 at 0.8, 0.11 at 1.2, 0.01 at 1.6 and -0.001 at 2.0. So the order melts away and the magnetization settles near zero. My Trotter circuits give nearly the same values (for example 0.742 at t=0.4).

What the test device gave back: the mock device does not simulate the circuit. It returned random-looking counts. Every circuit got about 25 percent each of just four bitstrings such as 000000 and 111111. The measured magnetization is about 0 at every time (between -0.03 and +0.01), including t=0, where a correct result is 1.0. So the mock only confirms that the job format and submission work. It cannot show physics. Only the ideal numbers above are the real physics answer.

What noise does on a real machine: every gate has a small error, and the circuits get deeper as time grows (20 slices at t=2). Errors and readout mistakes push the spins toward random, so the measured magnetization drifts toward 0 sooner than it should. Early points would be a bit too low. Late points are already near 0, so noise would hide the real small wiggles there. Longer simulations lose accuracy faster, which is why mitigation methods and better hardware matter for this use.
